item.title: Strengthening Cloud-Native Security Through Upstream Collaboration
item.dc:creator: Natalie Fisher
item.description:

The post Strengthening Cloud-Native Security Through Upstream Collaboration appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
Open source has always been foundational to cloud-native computing. Kubernetes itself is the product of thousands of contributors, but the platforms we build around it depend on an even broader ecosystem of projects spanning networking, storage, identity, backup and recovery, cluster lifecycle management, and more.

At Broadcom, contributing to that ecosystem has long meant more than consuming open source software. Our engineers contribute code, participate in communities, work alongside maintainers, and help projects evolve based on what we learn from running cloud-native technologies at enterprise scale.

Increasingly, we’re also thinking about another dimension of that responsibility: security.

The cloud-native world is expanding, and AI is shifting how we build and secure software. That opens up fresh ways to catch security risks while doubling down on what always works, which is direct, open collaboration with upstream communities.

Security Is a Shared Responsibility

Cloud-native infrastructure is inherently interconnected and a Kubernetes environment isn’t simply Kubernetes. It depends on projects responsible for cluster lifecycle, identity, storage, networking, backup and recovery, and many other capabilities. A security improvement in one of those projects can benefit far more than a single product or vendor.

That’s one reason we’ve expanded some of our upstream work to include proactive security research across open source projects that are important to the cloud-native ecosystem.

Our engineers work across projects including etcd, Cluster API, Pinniped, and Velero, where they work to identify potential issues, investigate them with project maintainers, and help move validated findings toward resolution.

The objective isn’t simply to find more vulnerabilities. It’s to help make the software that all of us depend on safer and more resilient.

Finding an Issue Is Only the Beginning

One thing this work has reinforced is that identifying a potential security issue and resolving one are very different things.

Modern AI tools can help engineers analyze large codebases and surface potential problems at a scale that would have been extraordinarily difficult through manual analysis alone. That’s a powerful capability, and one we believe can augment the work security researchers and software engineers are already doing.

But an AI-generated finding isn’t automatically a vulnerability.

Someone still has to understand the code. Is the behavior actually exploitable? Under what conditions? Which versions are affected? Is the proposed remediation appropriate? Could a fix introduce a regression somewhere else?

And in open source, there’s another critical participant in that process: the maintainer.

Maintainers understand the architecture, history, and operational realities of their projects. Responsible security work therefore requires collaboration by bringing potential findings to the appropriate project, validating them together, developing and reviewing fixes, and coordinating disclosure and releases when necessary.

AI can accelerate parts of that process. It doesn’t replace it.

From Findings to Upstream Fixes

We have seen the tangible impact of that upstream collaboration across several core projects: 

  • Velero: The work contributed directly to fixes for two published GitHub Security Advisories in the 1.18.3 release.
  • etcd: Research not only resolved issues across supported release branches but also updated the project’s threat model.
  • Cluster API and Pinniped: Findings were validated with community maintainers to deliver upstream remediations.

Project Highlights

  • Velero (v1.18.3): Coordinated and resolved security advisories GHSA-vrfp-2×59-hcfm and GHSA-8gv3-c356-fw76 upstream in release v1.18.3 (integrated downstream in VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) Add-ons v3.7.0+20260924), authoring patch remediation and performing end-to-end backup/restore validation.
  • etcd (v3.5.33 / v3.6.14 / v3.7.1): Discovered and disclosed CVE-2026-73500, contributed upstream patch remediation backported across releases v3.5.33, v3.6.14, and v3.7.1 (integrated downstream in vSphere Kubernetes Release (VKr) Oct Releases), and updated distributed state storage threat models.
  • Cluster API (v1.12.11, v1.13.5, v1.14.0): Screened and validated findings upstream, contributing bug fixes and hardening controller reconciliation logic.
  • Pinniped (v0.47.0): Identified authentication credential handling vulnerabilities under CVE-2026-59269, developed upstream remediation released in v0.47.0 (integrated downstream in VKr Oct Releases), and verified identity provider integration tests.

Impact by the Numbers

*Validated as Fixed Upstream: Pull Request with a fix was merged upstream and cherry picked when appropriate.

From AI Findings to Upstream Security Improvements

Identifying potential vulnerabilities is only the beginning. Turning AI-generated findings into meaningful security improvements requires careful validation, collaboration with upstream maintainers, and an understanding of each project’s architecture and threat model.

As Pushkar Joglekar, a Kubernetes maintainer who led this vulnerability discovery research, explained, an important part of the process was ensuring that findings were reviewed from a maintainer’s perspective before being shared with upstream projects.

“One non-negotiable requirement was to have every AI-generated finding filtered through a maintainer persona, so that when we request maintainer review time – a highly constrained resource – we are not wasting it by disclosing raw findings, which are often overstated or reflect intentional design decisions.”

This approach helped ensure that maintainer attention was focused on findings that warranted further investigation rather than potential issues already understood or accounted for in the project’s design.

For etcd, this collaboration also created opportunities to strengthen how security issues are evaluated. Benjamin Wang, an etcd maintainer, described how the work extended beyond validating vulnerabilities and developing patches to refining the project’s threat model and clarifying vulnerability boundaries.

These outcomes were not limited to identifying security vulnerabilities. In the Cluster API project, the research also provided opportunities to evaluate existing security practices and identify areas for additional hardening.

As longtime Cluster API maintainers Fabrizio Pandini and Stefan Büringer observed:

“Usage of AI models provides a new valuable source of input for this work, which led to a series of useful robustness / hardening improvements.”

They also emphasized that the absence of major findings reinforced the value of the project’s established security processes and ongoing collaboration with the Kubernetes Security Response Committee.

Together, these experiences demonstrate that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery is most valuable when paired with maintainer expertise and established upstream security practices. The result is not simply more findings, but better-informed security decisions and opportunities to strengthen the resilience of the projects the cloud-native ecosystem depends on.

Strengthening the Ecosystem We All Depend On

There is a tendency in technology to talk about open source contribution primarily in terms of features: a new capability contributed upstream, a new project donated to a foundation, or a new integration built with another project.

Those contributions matter.

But maintaining a healthy open source ecosystem also means doing some of the less visible work required to make that ecosystem dependable. This includes testing, reviewing, fixing, documenting, maintaining, and increasingly, proactively looking for ways to improve security.

For Broadcom, that’s an important part of what upstream participation means.

We build products using cloud-native open source technologies. Our customers rely on those technologies. Our engineers participate in the communities that maintain them.

When we combine our engineering expertise with emerging tools like AI to identify an issue, collaborate with maintainers, and contribute an improvement upstream, the benefit extends well beyond Broadcom.

It strengthens the shared foundation we’re all building on.

And as cloud-native infrastructure becomes the foundation for the next generation of applications and AI workloads, continuing to invest in that foundation may be one of the most important contributions we can make.

  • Running agent substrate on VKS
  • Advancing the Cloud-Native Ecosystem Through Open Collaboration

item.content:encoded:
Author: Tony Huynh, VCF Product Management

Selecting the right hardware for enterprise AI deployment can be a complex and daunting task. With VMware AI ReadyNodes, customers have a clear, reliable path to running Artificial Intelligence (AI) model fine-tuning and inference workloads on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). AI ReadyNodes are pre-validated, fully tested server systems designed to take the complexity out of hardware selection, helping guarantee seamless interoperability and effortless lifecycle management.

Why Choose VMware AI ReadyNodes? Key Customer Benefits

Deploying AI infrastructure requires high reliability, predictable performance, and smooth operational integration. The AI ReadyNode program delivers crucial advantages designed to accelerate your AI journey:

  • Rigorously Tested and Validated: OEM and ODM partners perform comprehensive validation across both servers and GPUs, helping ensure compatibility with VMware Cloud Foundation.
  • Purpose-Built for AI Workloads: Systems are explicitly certified with pre-qualified GPU hardware setups optimized specifically for intensive AI model fine-tuning and real-time inference tasks.
  • Zero Guesswork and Faster Time-to-Value: By choosing end-to-end validated configurations, organizations eliminate hardware trial-and-error, reducing setup risks and speeding up enterprise AI adoption.

Finding Certified Systems on the Broadcom Compatibility Guide

Broadcom simplified the process of identifying servers and GPUs that have been certified to run as VMware AI ReadyNodes systems. Use the Broadcom Compatibility Guide (BCG) to quickly explore valid configurations by clicking on the “AI Ready Node (Server + GPU)” section on the main page.

Figure 1. AI Ready Node (Server + GPU) option in Broadcom Compatibility Guide

Clicking on a specific server model opens a page that provides more details on the specific GPUs supported.

Figure 2. Details on AI ReadyNode Servers and GPUs supported

Figure 2 shows that this specific server has been certified with NVIDIA H100 NVL, NVIDIA H200 NVL, and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 series GPUs in both Direct Passthrough and vGPU mode.

Expanding Ecosystem and Future Outlook

The current list of AI Ready Nodes continues to grow as we work with OEMs and ODMs to certify new AI Servers and GPUs.

Figure 3. Certified AI Ready Nodes

Please refer to the AI Ready Node (Server + GPU) page on the BCG for the latest list of AI Ready Nodes.

The Path to AI ReadyNode Certification: Four Essential Steps

To earn the distinction of an AI ReadyNode, server vendors must successfully clear four stringent certification and functional testing phases to guarantee enterprise-grade performance and stability:

  1. vSphere Server Certification: Validates overall host server compatibility with vSphere through intensive stress benchmarks under simulated enterprise workloads.
  2. VM DirectPath I/O for General GPU (Passthrough): Helps ensure graphics processors can pass through directly to virtual machines (VMs) bypassing the hypervisor layer.
  3. DirectPath GPUs and Accelerators Certification: Certifies specialized vendor host drivers (such as NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel) to allow flexible GPU partitioning and multi-VM sharing within VCF.
  4. GPU Functional Testing on vSphere: Executes real-world functional tests recommended by NVIDIA and AMD for their respective GPUs.  

OEMs and ODMs complete the certification steps for vSphere Server Certification, VM DirectPath I/O for General GPU, and GPU functional testing on vSphere. Broadcom collaborates with GPU vendors to complete DirectPath GPU and Acceleration certification. 

Simply passing a subset of the certification/functional test above does not qualify a server as an AI ReadyNode; all certifications and functional tests need to be completed before a server is listed as an AI Ready Node. If a specific server and GPU are listed on the VM DirectPath I/O for General GPU page and not on the AI ReadyNode page, the GPU can be used for Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) and Financial (ML) Application workloads.

vSphere Server Certification

The vSphere Server certification program is a well-established initiative designed to verify complete hardware compatibility between vSphere and equipment from OEMs and ODMs. Certification involves a series of functional tests to confirm key capabilities, including:

  • ESX processor support
  • Successful ESX system boot functionality
  • Operation of specific operating systems (OS) on virtual machines (VMs)
  • Interoperability with supported virtual devices and their corresponding physical devices

Upon successfully passing these tests, qualified servers are published under the “System / Servers” section of the Broadcom Compatibility Guide (BCG).

VM DirectPath I/O for General GPU

All GPU-enabled servers are certified for VM DirectPath I/O for General GPU. Certification testing may be performed on Windows or Linux running a Graphics or Compute workload and validates that a GPU can be directly passed to a VM, bypassing the hypervisor. Customers can refer to the VM DirectPath I/O for General GPU page on the BCG, which will show a list of Server, GPU and ESX configurations certified to run ESX in DirectPath mode. The listing provides the supported Guest OS and GPU workload for a given server + GPU + ESX configuration. 

DirectPath GPU and Accelerators

Broadcom works with GPU vendors such as NVIDIA and AMD to validate and certify host drivers, which allow a GPU to be assigned to one or more virtual machines. With host drivers, customers get additional visibility into the device and operational flexibility with VCF with capabilities like GPU sharing with multiple VMs, and providing deeper operational insights into the GPU through management tools such as vCenter and VCF Operations. An entry in this does not mean that the GPU is available for consumption with a server. Based on the use case, the user needs to refer to either the AI ReadyNode listing or VMDirectPath I/O for General GPUs listing to figure out which server this GPU is certified with. The list of GPUs and certified host drivers can be found on the DirectPath GPUs and Accelerators page. Please note that this page also includes hardware accelerators that are not GPUs, which are outside the scope of this blog.

GPU Functional Tests on vSphere

After completing the certifications listed above, OEM and ODM vendors execute GPU functional tests on vSphere, including:

  • Real-world functional tests recommended by NVIDIA and AMD for their respective GPUs.
  • Testing NVIDIA GPUs in DirectPath and vGPU modes, and AMD GPUs in DirectPath and Enhanced DirectPath modes.

Before executing GPU functional tests on vSphere, vendors must run bare-metal server and GPU performance tests from the GPU vendors. For example, the NVIDIA-Certified Systems program ensures systems are optimized for enterprise-grade performance, manageability, scalability, and security for AI and accelerated computing applications.

item.title: Beat the Ticking Clock: Continuous Security in the Era of AI Exploits
item.dc:creator: brandon hahn
item.description:
Every time a new vulnerability is discovered, a silent clock starts ticking. It signals the start of a race between your infrastructure team and global threat actors. Does your organization have the technology and processes in place to resolve or mitigate a vulnerability in your environment before an attacker can compromise? And not just once. … Continued

The post Beat the Ticking Clock: Continuous Security in the Era of AI Exploits appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
Every time a new vulnerability is discovered, a silent clock starts ticking. It signals the start of a race between your infrastructure team and global threat actors. Does your organization have the technology and processes in place to resolve or mitigate a vulnerability in your environment before an attacker can compromise? And not just once. Not on a schedule. Whenever and whatever technology happens to have been impacted this time. Adding to the fun, these clocks are starting to tick a lot more often. According to Zero Day Clock, year to date 2026 we’re on track to have double the number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) issued than in 2025.

Figure 1. Source: Zero Day Clock (https://zerodayclock.com)

This massive acceleration isn’t a fluke; it is the direct result of Frontier AI. Advanced AI models are now routinely weaponized by threat actors to ingest vast codebases, identify deep architectural flaws, and automate the creation of exploit code in record time. This AI-driven exploit engine has fuelled a massive explosion in the sheer number of published CVEs, fundamentally lowering the barrier to entry for attackers. As one of my Engineering professors often said, “Once the smoke has left the diode you can never get it back in.” This is our brave new world; there’s no going back.

You cannot win an AI-accelerated footrace if you are weighed down by traditional IT operations. If applying a critical hypervisor security update requires three weeks of change-control meetings, navigating maintenance windows, large scale vMotion events, and coordinating time consuming server reboots, you have already lost the race. Your infrastructure remains critically exposed while the organization negotiates precious downtime.

To beat attackers today, your defensive speed must outpace their offensive automation. Staying current on patches can no longer be a disruptive, high-friction event. It must be immediate, painless, and completely invisible to the workloads running on top of it. VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.1 removes the massive headache of scheduling downtime, letting you patch vulnerabilities the same day patches drop. That’s how you stand a chance to actually win the race.

Rapid and Seamless Patching

Zero-Downtime ESXi Live Patching

The most significant weapon in the new lifecycle arsenal is the dramatic expansion of ESXi Live Patching. VCF 9.1.1 allows administrators to update core vmkernel components and user-space daemons, including vital vSAN and storage libraries, without rebooting the host or entering maintenance mode. This extends even to TPM-enabled servers. The hypervisor can seamlessly swap out vulnerable code for patched code while virtual machines continue running smoothly, entirely unaware that the underlying hypervisor has just been updated and secured. This is a massive win from a security perspective. Critical hypervisor zero-days can now be remediated in hours rather than weeks.

Patching vCenter in Under a Minute

This zero-downtime approach doesn’t stop at the hosts. It now applies to vCenter too. Historically, patching vCenter required taking the vSphere management plane offline, temporarily blinding administrators and halting automated provisioning pipelines. With vCenter Quick Patch in VCF 9.1.1, the platform targets only the specific binaries containing code changes rather than replacing the entire appliance image.

This surgical approach drops management plane patching downtime to under a minute and in many cases, achieves true zero downtime. API endpoints remain responsive, infrastructure-as-code deployments continue uninterrupted, and the control plane is secured without causing a disruption to the business. Even in cases where vCenter Quick Patch isn’t available, vCenter Reduced Downtime Upgrade is still available to minimize the impact to the management plane.

Continuous Security

By eliminating the operational friction of patching, infrastructure teams no longer have to push back on security mandates. Security delivery becomes a continuous, non-disruptive background process rather than a high-stress, anxiety inducing, 2 a.m. outage-required event after defending the need for these patches to yet another Change Advisory Board. The combination of vCenter Quick Patch and ESXi Live Patch nearly eliminates the technical friction of patching the vSphere management plane. Don’t forget to modernize your organization’s operational policies to take advantage of these game changing technologies.

Streamlined Centralized Lifecycle Management

Historically, applying a security patch to a complex virtualization environment meant waiting for a massive, monolithic update. When a critical vulnerability was disclosed, security teams were often forced to wait while vendors bundled the fix into a larger maintenance release, which then required extensive regression testing across the entire stack. VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1 changes this paradigm entirely with the introduction of Express Patches, decoupling critical security fixes from heavy feature releases.

Agile, Targeted Remediation

Express Patches are lightweight, highly targeted updates designed specifically for rapid CVE remediation. Rather than deploying gigabytes of updated binaries that touch every part of the system, Express Patches deliver only the precise code needed to close a security gap. This dramatically reduces the testing burden on IT Operations and shrinks the Time-to-Remediate (TTR) from weeks or months down to days.

Removing the Patch Sequencing Bottleneck

In previous architectures, patching required strict adherence to a validated upgrade sequence. If you wanted to patch one component, you often had to upgrade several others in a specific order to maintain compatibility. VCF 9.1.1 eliminates this friction for management components. Unless specifically noted in the release notes, Express Patches for VCF Management Services can be applied independently and in any order, completely removing the sequencing overhead that traditionally delayed emergency patching.

Centralized and Intelligent Patch Deployment

This new agile patching model is driven entirely through the centralized Build > Lifecycle dashboard in VCF Operations. The platform automatically checks for, downloads, and stages available patches, including Express Patches. More importantly, the system’s intelligent automation evaluates the incoming patch payload for the entire VCF Stack. If a patch contains fixes that are Live Patch or Quick Patch Eligible, VCF automatically routes it through the non-disruptive patching technologies discussed earlier.

Figure 2. VCF Management Services Patching

Figure 3. VCF Component Upgrade Planning

The result is a patching lifecycle where emergency security updates are pulled down automatically, require no complex sequence planning, and are applied surgically without taking down workloads or the management plane.

Core Security Enhancements

While rapid patching closes newly discovered vulnerabilities, a truly secure infrastructure requires a hardened baseline that refuses to degrade over time. VCF 9.1.1 bakes security hygiene directly into the platform’s day-two operations, automating the tedious tasks that traditionally lead to configuration drift and operational outages.

Managing Certificates Without the Spreadsheets

Expired certificates are one of the most common causes of preventable infrastructure outages and security warnings. VCF 9.1.1 takes the manual labor—and the human error—out of this critical process. By default, during management plane upgrades, the platform automatically evaluates the VMCA root certificate and subsequent solution user certificates. If they are within a year of expiration, VCF automatically renews them in the background. This helps ensure the trust boundary remains intact without requiring administrators to track spreadsheets of expiration dates or execute manual key rotations.

Secured Down to the Physical Infrastructure

Physical security and boot integrity are no longer manual checklist items. VCF 9.1.1 deeply integrates secure cluster lifecycle management with Secure Boot and TPM architectures. When new hosts are added or existing nodes are restarted, the platform automatically validates the hardware configuration and boot state. This ensures that no unauthorized hypervisor modifications or bootkits can compromise the underlying infrastructure before workloads are even deployed, enforcing zero-trust principles at the bare-metal layer.

Continuously Secure Configurations

A secure deployment is only secure until an administrator tweaks a setting for troubleshooting and forgets to revert it. To combat configuration drift, VCF 9.1.1 embeds desired state management directly into the cluster lifecycle using vSphere Configuration Profiles. Whenever a cluster receives an update or a host is rebooted, the system automatically enforces the defined desired state – including the ability to set advanced hypervisor security parameters, locking down SSH, and validating vSAN settings. This guarantees that your secure baseline is actively maintained, remediating drift automatically without relying on external day-two scripting.

Staying Secure

The AI-driven threat landscape will only continue to accelerate, but defending your infrastructure no longer has to be a disruptive, organizational battle. VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1 has advanced enterprise security by removing the top sources of friction that have historically paralyzed IT operations.

By eliminating the operational penalties of patching—maintenance windows, host evacuations, and the risks of rebooting—ESXi Live Patching, vCenter Quick Patches, and VCF Express Patches empower your security and infrastructure teams to remediate zero-days at the actual speed of the modern threat cycle. Coupled with automated certificate management and strictly enforced configuration profiles, the platform ensures that once your secure baseline is established, it remains permanently hardened against drift.

You no longer have to compromise between continuous uptime and continuous security. Upgrading to VCF 9.1.1 is more than an infrastructure modernization effort; it is the strategic pivot that gives your organization the speed, agility, and automation required to finally win the race against modern threat actors.

item.title: How VM API and KubeVM Service Deliver Open Standards and Enterprise Execution
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
VMs are the foundation of enterprise computing. They run the majority of mission-critical production workloads today, and they will continue to do so for years to come. What is changing is how platform engineering teams want to operate them. As organizations build internal developer platforms around Kubernetes, teams want a single, declarative operating model across … Continued

The post How VM API and KubeVM Service Deliver Open Standards and Enterprise Execution appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
VMs are the foundation of enterprise computing. They run the majority of mission-critical production workloads today, and they will continue to do so for years to come. What is changing is how platform engineering teams want to operate them.

As organizations build internal developer platforms around Kubernetes, teams want a single, declarative operating model across their entire footprint. They want self-service provisioning, GitOps automation, and policy-as-code applied everywhere. If a team needs declarative VM management, they need an open, standardized way to do it, without fragmenting their tooling or introducing vendor lock-in at the API layer. That is exactly why Broadcom announced on November 9, 2026, that the VM API project has been officially accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox.

Making Declarative VM Management Open: The VM API Initiative

The VM API project is not an untested prototype. It builds directly on VM Operator, a project with more than six years of continuous enterprise development and production mileage inside VMware vSphere, handling the real-world complexities of Day-2 operations, dynamic networking, and hardware reconciliation.

The architectural approach for VM API draws inspiration from the Cluster API (CAPI) model. Just as CAPI established a standard framework for platform teams to declaratively provision and manage Kubernetes clusters across different infrastructure backends, VM API aims to apply that same proven architectural pattern to VMs. It establishes a standardized, provider-neutral API contract for virtual workloads.

  • Standard CRDs (Portable Intent): Developers define their VM requirements using familiar Kubernetes YAML manifests.
  • Pluggable Providers: Behind that single API contract, provider plugins execute operations on the target infrastructure. While VM API serves as the common abstraction layer, different providers will have different advantages and trade-offs depending on their execution environment.

A Unified API Across On-Prem and Cloud

A core advantage of VM API is that it allows platform engineers to abstract VM operations across various supported providers. Instead of forcing teams to learn different APIs for on-premises infrastructure and public clouds, VM API provides developers with a consistent management interface and portable intent. While you can deploy the identical declarative YAML specification across any supported environment, the specific features, performance, and operational outcomes will depend on the underlying provider executing that request.

This declarative intent is then realized as real VMs on the backend. For on-premises, this could be KubeVM Service provisioning native ESX VMs on vSphere, or other potential plugins for environments like Proxmox on KVM. For the public cloud, plugins can provision EC2 instances on AWS or VMs on Google Cloud.

Note: The chart and table below illustrates these potential options to demonstrate the architecture. It does not represent all currently available providers. Please check the active CNCF Sandbox repository to see the official list of supported providers.

Why This Matters for New AI Applications

The push for declarative VM management is highly driven by the explosion of Generative AI. As developers build autonomous AI agents and complex indexing pipelines, these workloads frequently execute untrusted third-party code or process highly confidential proprietary models. Standard containers share the host operating system kernel, which can expose the underlying infrastructure to security risks when dealing with untrusted agentic AI tasks.

The advantage here is not that containers are inherently less secure, but that moving to containerized boundaries often requires organizations to re-architect their implementation, redesigning firewall rules, network segmentation, and compliance auditing around pod constructs. By bridging VMs into the Kubernetes ecosystem via VM API, platform teams provide hypervisor-enforced isolation boundaries for workloads with elevated security requirements while continuing to leverage established, audited, VM-centric security processes and tooling without reinventing the wheel. Data scientists get the declarative, self-service GitOps experience they expect for GPU-accelerated AI workstations, while enterprise security teams maintain complete operational continuity.

KubeVM Service: Selective Modernization on Existing Investments

While VM API provides the universal open standard for requesting a VM, KubeVM Service is the commercial vSphere provider that fulfills that request natively on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF).

We want to be clear: there is absolutely nothing wrong with traditional vSphere VMs, and they are here to stay. However, if you want to provide a modern, cloud-native experience for teams developing these new AI applications, KubeVM Service allows you to selectively enable this declarative experience directly on your existing VCF investment. For a deeper dive into how this operates, read our recent post, Introducing KubeVM Service.

By leveraging KubeVM Service as your VM API provider, you get the best of both worlds:

  • Frictionless GitOps: Developers manage VMs just like containers using standard Kubernetes workflows.
  • Operational Continuity: The same VM remains visible to vCenter, VCF Operations, and existing backup tooling. VI admins retain their established governance and guardrails.
  • Enterprise Resilience: Workloads benefit from native vSphere HA, DRS, and vMotion, completely abstracting hardware failures away from the Kubernetes layer.

The Numbers: Why Unified Operations Matter

To benchmark how platform teams are balancing their infrastructure, Broadcom and the CNCF sponsored a Linux Foundation Survey in September 2026, gathering data from 492 practitioners. The findings confirm that VMs remain central to modern enterprise architecture:

  • VMs remain the core footprint: The average organization runs 53% of its production applications on VMs, with only 10% reporting zero production VMs.
  • Operational teams are merging: 61% of respondents report that their VM administrators and container/platform teams are now collaborative or fully integrated.
  • AI workloads demand hardware-grade isolation: Among organizations expanding VM capacity, 34% cite AI and agentic workloads as a primary driver, prompting teams to lean into hardware-level isolation for untrusted third-party code.

Advancing the Ecosystem Through Open Collaboration

The contribution of VM API aligns with Broadcom’s broader strategy to strengthen the cloud-native ecosystem through upstream collaboration. Alongside the VM API Sandbox acceptance, Broadcom also announced it is co-chairing the newly formed Workload Conformance Working Group within the Kubernetes community. While programs exist today to certify Kubernetes platforms, this new working group aims to establish common, verifiable expectations for how workloads behave, reducing validation efforts for enterprise platform teams and ISVs across heterogeneous environments.

Furthermore, the ecosystem supporting these workloads is expanding rapidly. VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) recently validated more than 20 new partner solutions, spanning observability, security, and storage, giving customers greater flexibility when deploying both containers and VMs.

For more details on these initiatives, read the official press release and the companion open collaboration blog.

Get Involved

Platform teams aren’t looking to abandon their virtualization platforms. They want to bring declarative, Kubernetes-native workflows to those environments so developers have a single, automated interface for compute.

We invite the platform engineering community to help shape this evolution.

  • Test KubeVM Service: Experience the commercial vSphere provider firsthand by enabling it on your existing VCF deployments.
  • Contribute to VM API: View the specification, explore the different providers, and contribute code in the VM API GitHub repository within the CNCF Sandbox.

item.content:encoded:
The shift towards AI is pushing cloud-native infrastructure into new territory, creating architectural demands, such as hardened sandboxes and burstable execution, that Kubernetes was not originally designed to meet. AI agents work in short bursts separated by long stretches of waiting for a model, a tool or a human response. Throughout these pauses, they continue holding state in memory and on disk. At the same time, agents also execute untrusted code, demanding hardened sandbox isolation. When workloads scale from thousands of long-lived pods to millions of ephemeral agents, standard primitives hit an all triggering IP exhaustion, routing churn and unsustainable cost of holding the compute resources.

Agent Substrate, an open-source CNCF project, solves the problem by providing a high density, secure runtime and scheduling framework for running AI agents at scale on Kubernetes. It multiplexes thousands of sandboxed, mostly idle agents onto a minimal pool of shared compute by rapid snapshotting, hibernating, and resuming their execution states on demand. The project aims to snapshot agent states under 100ms via incremental snapshots, achieving 10x higher compute density, and support over 1 million concurrent actors.

(More on Agent Substrate: https://ate.dev/)

Just as Kubernetes schedules pods onto nodes, Agent Substrate schedules Actors into worker pods. An Actor is the actual agent workload. But unlike a pod, an actor isn’t permanently pinned to physical infrastructure or bound to a continuous container lifecycle. When an actor needs to run, Agent Substrate schedules it into a warm pod running on a kubernetes node. The moment it goes idle, Substrate flushes a full memory and filesystem snapshot to fast storage, instantly freeing that worker pod to execute other workloads. Through Actor Teleport, when an event or response arrives, that actor can be scheduled onto any available worker in the pool, picking up execution seamlessly without losing state. Kubernetes handles what it does best: node provisioning, autoscaling, and worker recovery. Meanwhile, Substrate’s dedicated control and data plane handle actor scheduling and fast suspend-resume cycles.

Today, Agent Substrate relies on runtimes like gVisor for software-level isolation, optimizing for density and immediate startup. However, emerging AI workloads have diverse risk profiles that demand a broader spectrum of isolation options ranging from lightweight sandboxes to strict hardware boundaries. To support this we are exploring hardware assisted isolation models, including potential future integration with vSphere Pods, with running workers inside lightweight, dedicated Virtual Machines (VMs) would enforce zero-trust hardware isolation, while nesting gVisor inside these PodVMs would still preserve sub-millisecond sandbox creation.

This blog covers four areas: 

  • What a VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) add-on gives you
  • Packaging an open-source project as a VKS add-on
  • Installing the add-on on a VKS Cluster
  • A live demo of actor suspension, snapshotting, and cross-worker resumption

What a VKS add-on gives you

A quick note before diving in: while VKS supports add-on extensibility, the specific add-on, manifests, and artifacts shared in this post are intended solely for demonstration. The artifacts featured here are not officially supported, and these examples should not be treated as supported production configurations. You can learn more about VKS add-ons here. 

As teams bring emerging open-source AI frameworkers into production, the VKS add-on framework provides a standardized, fleet-wide model to integrate, configure and lifecycle manage them. Rather than treating each tool as an add-hoc operation silo, VKS turns complex open-source components into first class citizens of VKS.

  • Catalog Entry
    An Addon in the Supervisor.
  • One configuration API
    An AddonConfigDefinition holds the schema, defaults and bounds. Users set per-cluster values in an AddonConfig.
  • Fleet rollout by labels and constraints
    An AddonInstall selects the clusters using label selectors or constraints defined using CEL expressions.
  • Per-cluster status
    A ClusterAddon shows the release and whether it’s Ready.
  • Declared compatibility
    A Kubernetes version constraint on the package, here >=1.37.0 <1.38.0.
  • Managed lifecycle
    The add-on is reconciled continuously and self-heals. VKS add-ons integrate well with Cluster API (CAPI): when the cluster upgrades, the add-on is updated to the latest release that is compatible with the constraints it defines, unless a release is pinned for the cluster allowing upgrade to be managed explicitly.

Everything is declarative YAML, so it fits GitOps. Users don’t have to learn each project’s own installer, and admins get one workflow for every add-on. The VKS documentation describes the model in full: Managing Add-ons in VKS Clusters.

Packaging Agent Substrate as a Helm add-on

Substrate ships install manifests (Deployments, DaemonSets and the like), not Helm charts. VKS add-ons natively support both Carvel and Helm packaging formats, we chose Helm for Agent Substrate to leverage standard Helm chart tooling. Here is how you can create the add-on:

Leverage eisting Helm Chart KAgent
We have leveraged kagent helm chart which packages the broader agent stack and integrates Agent Substrate as the underlying execution engine

Expose Helm Values Schema
Ten core values are exposed through standard Helm values.yaml and typed via values.schema.json: replica counts, storage sizes, token issuer, and other parameters.

Parameterize Manifests
Standard Helm templating constructs map user configuration directly into resource manifests and coordinate deployment sequencing.

Package and Publish
We published the Helm chart as an OCI artifact and declared the package metadata in the catalog namespace.

The commands from here on use three helpers:

Publishing puts three resources in the catalog namespace on the Supervisor. Addon is a metadata object: a description, a display name and similar information. It’s the catalog entry:

AddonRelease is one version of the add-on, here Substrate v0.5.0, together with its Kubernetes compatibility constraints:

AddonConfigDefinition holds the configuration schema and the configuration templating for one release of the add-on. The template turns a cluster’s settings into a value Secret for the package. Ours defines ten values. This is a trimmed copy:

Packaging Agent Substrate as a standard Helm chart makes it seamlessly compatible with VKS add-on management while retaining standard Helm configuration workflows.

Installing the add-on

Installing using VCFA UI

Agent substrate can be installed from the addons catalog in the VCFA UI.

Installing using Command Line

An AddonInstall selects clusters with labels and with constraints written as CEL expressions. This one selects a fleet of clusters by matching labels:

Settings for one cluster go in an AddonConfig, validated against the schema. This one asks for one API replica and ten workers:

A ClusterAddon represents the add-on for one workload cluster and reports its status there. Once a cluster is selected, VKS installs the add-on, and when the ClusterAddon says Ready, Substrate is running:

In the workload cluster, the package brought up the control plane, the routers, a pool of ten workers, RustFS and an atelet on the node. A second namespace holds the certificate controller:

Actors run under gVisor. The script checks the sandbox configuration and the worker image:

The demo

The following demonstration explores Agent Substrate in VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) environment: https://youtu.be/mDfZmFEvCdw.

Four-agent multiplexing and egress policy

Fleet Setup

To showcase multi-tenant isolation, routing, and density, we create a shared atespace named vks-demo and instantiate four distinct actors Luna, Mars, Orion, and Vega from a standard agent template. Fine-grained egress network policies are attached to enforce strict endpoint access per actor: Luna and Mars are restricted exclusively to Anthropic model endpoints, while Orion and Vega route solely to OpenAI.

Execution and Lifecycle

All four actors are multiplexed onto just two worker pods in the pool. When incoming requests arrive, the atelet router schedules Luna and Orion to active worker pods. Inside each worker, gVisor intercepts system calls in user space, enforcing secure sandbox isolation for untrusted code execution. As soon as an actor pauses or completes a turn, Substrate captures an incremental memory and filesystem snapshot to fast storage and hibernates the actor, instantly freeing worker pods to process subsequent actor workloads. When a new event arrives, Substrate seamlessly resumes the actor on any available worker pod in under 200ms on an average (depending on available bandwidth and the actor’s memory footprint) without losing execution state.

Addressing the complex requirements of modern AI demands an architectural framework built across multiple operational layers as cloud-native environments expand. Novel developments like the VM API extend standard Kubernetes control planes to govern lower-level compute components, whereas Agent Substrate focuses on handling the distinct isolation, scheduling, and state requirements inherent to agentic systems. By leveraging VKS as a unified enterprise foundation, operators can easily deploy, configure, and manage these open-source tools across entire fleets. Showcasing these capabilities highlights our ongoing focus on evolving core Kubernetes primitives equipping platform teams with a robust infrastructure designed to support dense, highly isolated AI workloads safely at scale.

item.title: VCF Firewall Planner Tool: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough from 1,063 Candidate Rules to 224
item.dc:creator: syed qamar
item.description:
Most published VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) flows never need a firewall rule. The VCF Firewall Planner takes the full Broadcom port catalogue for VCF 9.1 and, in 12 guided steps, cuts it down to the consolidated rule set your design needs. Every exclusion keeps its reason, so the firewall team can see why a flow … Continued

The post VCF Firewall Planner Tool: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough from 1,063 Candidate Rules to 224 appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
Most published VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) flows never need a firewall rule. The VCF Firewall Planner takes the full Broadcom port catalogue for VCF 9.1 and, in 12 guided steps, cuts it down to the consolidated rule set your design needs. Every exclusion keeps its reason, so the firewall team can see why a flow was left out, not only that it was.

For the ACME assessment used in this walkthrough, the numbers are:

Why the Raw ports.vmware.com Rule Set Is Hard to Use

The Broadcom ports catalogue lists every port for every product. That’s what a reference should do, but it isn’t a firewall design. Each row below is a problem I’ve encountered on real engagements, and the planner step that fixes it.

The 12 Steps

What follows is a live run of the ACME assessment. For each step you get the screen, the problem it solves, and what it changed.

Step 1: Start with the Customer

The problem: the catalogue is one generic list for every customer, with no per-engagement record of the decisions you made.

Name the customer and add a short description of the environment. Each assessment is saved and you can pick it again from the sidebar. The left rail tracks your progress through all 12 steps. Here, the ACME assessment is created.

Step 2: Choose the Network Model

The problem: the rules don’t say which VLAN or subnet each endpoint sits on, so there’s no mapping to the design.

There are four models to choose from: shared, dedicated, overlay and stretched. ACME uses VCF Management Dedicated Subnet. A live diagram shows which components sit on which VLAN, and the model you pick drives the Layer 2 and gateway logic later on.

Step 3: Select the Products in Scope

The problem: the catalogue covers every VCF product, whether you deploy it or not.

Products are grouped into Core, Management and Consumption, and each one shows its rule entries and the VLANs it touches. ACME selects 9 of 13 products. Products that aren’t deployed, such as vSAN and HCX, drop out.

Step 4: Switch On the Add-Ons You Deploy

The problem: the list carries rules for add-ons the customer never deployed, such as vDefend or DSM.

ACME turns on two of nine add-ons, which claim 157 entries: the VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) cluster and Avi Load Balancer. VMware vDefend, Data Services Manager (DSM), vSphere Replication, and the rest stay off. Each add-on lists the VLANs its flows use.

Step 5: Pick the Shared Infra Services

The problem: the catalogue assumes every shared service exists, including DHCP, SNMP, Mail, KMS, and PTP.

ACME includes 5 of 10 services: AD, DNS, NTP, Syslog and Backup. DHCP, SNMP, Mail, KMS, and PTP are excluded. You can include or exclude everything in one click.

Step 6: Turn Off Unused Features

The problem: nothing links a rule to the feature it serves, so you can’t drop rules for features you don’t use.

Every flow is mapped to its Broadcom purpose. ACME keeps 189 of 239 features. vCenter HA, Enhanced Linked Mode, and KMIP are off. By this point 149 rules are excluded.

Step 7: Set the Gateway per VLAN

The problem: the list includes rules for traffic that never reaches a firewall, because both VLANs route on the ToR.

Mark each VLAN as routed on the ToR or on the firewall. For ACME, 9 VLANs route on the ToR and 34 on the firewall. Flows with both ends on the ToR never reach the firewall, so they go. TEP-to-TEP flows are removed automatically.

Step 8: Consolidate the Rules

The problem: one line per port means hundreds of near-duplicate lines in the change request.

One line per port becomes one rule per flow. Ports and protocols are merged per source and destination. For ACME, 662 lines merge into 282, saving 380 lines. The rulebook opens in the consolidated view.

Step 9: Add AI-Suggested Egress Rules

The problem: internet URLs for the depot, licensing and HCL sit in KB articles and TechDocs, not in the catalogue, and they change.

The AI engine reads Broadcom KB articles and TechDocs as well as the ports catalogue. It finds internet egress such as dl.broadcom.com and eapi.broadcom.com on TCP 443. When Broadcom updates a KB or a doc, the next run picks up the change. For ACME it adds 15 rules from 18 hosts. You can toggle each suggestion, and it’s tagged once in the rulebook.

Step 10: Answer the Design Considerations

The problem: every customer has its own exclusions, such as no overlay, no VI workload domain, or an offline or proxied depot.

Four design questions switch whole groups of flows on or off:

  • VI workload domain flows: 294 entries
  • Overlay networking: 57 entries
  • IPsec and BGP peering: 8 entries
  • VCF Installer depot: online, offline or via proxy

Step 11: Remove Layer 2 Same-VLAN Flows

The problem: the list has rules for flows inside the same VLAN, which never cross a firewall.

For ACME, 213 entries stay inside a VLAN and 507 cross a boundary and need a rule. If the design differs from the model, you can remap a component’s VLAN. After this step the included rules drop to 224.

Step 12: Review Every Exclusion

The problem: there’s no record of why a rule was left out, so reviewers can’t validate it.

The exclusion summary lists 559 excluded rules, each with its reason. For ACME, that covers 4 products, 5 infra services, 7 add-ons, 23 features and 2 ToR boundaries. Save your changes to publish the rulebook.

Results: 1,063 Rules Down to 224

This is what the customer gets at the end of the assessment, shown for ACME on network Model 2.

Roadmap: Map Your IP/CIDRs from the P&P Workbook to the Rule Set

Today you still copy addresses from the Planning and Preparation workbook into the change request by hand. The next feature removes that step.

RoadmapComing soon

No more copying addresses by hand from the workbook into the change request.

Get Started

Get started

The planner is at ports.vcf9.ai. Sign in with your company email, and if it’s your first time, click Register. Port data comes from the Broadcom ports catalogue, KB articles, and TechDocs.

How to Log In

The planner runs at ports.vcf9.ai. You need a work email address. Your account is created the first time you register.

Login 1: Open the Planner

Go to ports.vcf9.ai. The sign-in page opens. If this is your first visit, click Register. If you already have an account, skip to Login 3.

Login 2: Register on First Use

Enter your first name, last name and work email address. The planner generates a password for you. It is shown once, so click Show or Copy and save it before you go on. Click Authenticate, then enter the six-digit code sent to your email to confirm the address.

Login 3: Sign In

Enter your work email address and the password you saved at registration, then click Sign in. The planner opens on the assessment list, where you start at Step 1.

Use it on your next project

Have a VCF 9.1 design coming up? Run its firewall planning through the VCF Firewall Planner before the first rule request goes to the firewall team. Build the assessment for your customer, take the consolidated rule set and the exclusion summary into the design review, and give the firewall team a list where every rule has a reason.

Then tell me what would make it better. If a step doesn’t match how your customer builds VCF, a flow looks wrong, or you want another export or check, leave a comment on this post or send me a note.

Open the VCF Firewall Planner

item.dc:creator: audrey bian
item.description:
Enterprises are facing challenges when it comes to modernizing applications. How do we modernize applications without losing the control, security, and performance of private cloud? item.content:encoded:
Enterprises are facing challenges when it comes to modernizing applications. How do we modernize applications without losing the control, security, and performance of private cloud? Teams need to ship features faster, adopt microservices and AI workloads, and retire technical debt, all on infrastructure they trust. The market rewards speed, and organizations that modernize well gain agility and competitive advantage.

The core problem is not ambition. It is the gap between where applications run today and the operational model needed to support what comes next. Many organizations juggle fragmented tooling, manual provisioning, and disjointed governance across traditional and cloud-native workloads. That fragmentation slows delivery, raises risk, and drives up cost.

A Standardized, Secure Path to Production

VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) closes that gap with a consistent, secure private cloud that supports all applications. As the leading private cloud platform for application modernization, VCF gives organizations the platform to modernize their application portfolio without abandoning the control and security of private cloud. With Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) certified built-in Kubernetes runtime delivered through VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS), VCF transforms private cloud into a modern platform that delivers the agility of public cloud with the governance and hardened security your business demands.

Let’s look at what this means in practice. The platform delivers several capabilities that directly improve operational outcomes:

  • A complete platform to securely deploy and manage modern applications at scale through three core services: KubeVM Service, VKS, and Container Service.
  • Self-service access through CLI and Kubernetes APIs and GUI, empowering application teams to provision VMs, Kubernetes clusters, and containers on demand without waiting on IT tickets.
  • Native integrations with CNCF tools like Argo CD, enabling source-controlled GitOps workflows without replacing what already works.
  • Unified lifecycle management that streamlines provisioning, patching, and upgrades across the stack.
  • Automated governance and security guardrails across infrastructure, enabling consistent policy enforcement and rapid remediation without slowing innovation.

Operational Insight: Where Velocity Meets Control

The friction in app modernization is familiar to most platform teams. Developers want self-service speed. Security and operations teams want control and consistency. Too often, one comes at the expense of the other.

VCF resolves this by making governance part of the automation, not a gate in front of it. VCF Automation acts as the central orchestration engine, dynamically applying security and compliance postures at deployment time. By defining network and security constructs within blueprints, platform teams enable a zero-trust policy that is consistently codified across every environment. VCF optimized Ubuntu operating system image delivery locks image sourcing to verified repositories, so every team works from trusted, standardized content.

For total cost of ownership (TCO), the math is straightforward. A single platform that supports traditional and modern workloads reduces the need to maintain separate stacks. VCF Automation drives down capital expenditures (CapEx) through automated lease expirations and resource reclamation, while built-in cost tracking dashboards give application teams real-time visibility into running costs. VCF Operations reduce operational expenditure (OpEx) by consolidating management, automating lifecycle tasks, and giving teams the visibility to act before costs compound. A Broadcom survey1 of VCF 9 customers found an average 51% reduction in infrastructure management time and a 46% reduction in monitoring time, driven by a single converged console that unifies metrics, logs, and flows. 

VCF streamlines AI model deployment by integrating automated data preparation, standardized API access, simplified agent deployment, and full stack observability into a unified platform. VCF Automation transforms complex AI infrastructure into on-demand, consumable services. By publishing pre-configured AI infrastructure blueprints through a self-service catalog, platform teams eliminate manual provisioning bottlenecks. Developers instantly receive standardized environments, fully configured with the necessary compute and guardrails, allowing them to focus entirely on rapid model development and cost-effective CPU-based inferencing.  Developers can compose AI agents that run flexibly on CPUs or GPUs, allowing cost-effective CPU deployment when dedicated GPUs aren’t required. 

Broadcom’s Contribution in CNCF Community 

This commitment extends beyond the platform itself. Broadcom has been a top three contributor to Kubernetes for the past decade and recently elevated to Platinum membership in the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). Broadcom’s presence at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City, November 9 to 12, underscores this commitment. Broadcom returns as a Platinum Sponsor and supports Cloud Native AI + Inference Day on November 9 as a Diamond Sponsor. 

Broadcom’s broad independent software vendor (ISV) partnerships extend the platform’s compatibility and reach, so teams can build on a foundation that grows with their needs. At KubeCon, Broadcom announced the latest wave of partner validations for VKS and its contribution to the VM API, a common, provider-neutral standard for managing virtual machines across infrastructure environments.

This track record runs deeper than membership and sponsorships. Broadcom originated CNCF projects including Harbor, Antrea, Velero, and Contour, and maintains core projects such as Cluster API, etcd, containerd, Kubernetes CSI, and controller-runtime. These contributions reflect a sustained investment in open source innovation and the technologies powering the next generation of cloud native and AI workloads.

Beyond Infrastructure: The secure platform for agents

VMware Tanzu Platform extends the value of VCF, giving teams a dedicated application platform that turns infrastructure capability into developer productivity for modern applications and agents.

App Portfolio Assessment and Compliance 

VMware Tanzu Platform enables teams to scan application repositories at scale, analyzing each one for technical debt, business criticality, and language to build a complete picture of the portfolio. It identifies specific risks such as unpatched dependencies or unsupported frameworks that are often hidden in the maintenance tax of production environments. Platform engineers can then prioritize workloads for patching and onboarding based on objective metrics, eliminating latent security risks before they become incidents. The result is a data-driven modernization roadmap that strengthens the organization’s security posture and helps improve app portfolio compliance through continuous, automated assessment rather than manual audits. 

Agentic Runtimes for Autonomous Agents 

VMware Tanzu Platform provides an Agentic Platform as a Service (PaaS) with Spring AI integration, centralized Model Context Protocol (MCP) management, and identity-driven governance to help teams build and govern agentic applications. Organizations can deploy and scale autonomous AI agents on a deny-by-default runtime with brokered service bindings to curated models, data products and services, isolated sandboxes, and deterministic compliance controls. 

Defense-in-depth for Apps and Agents 

Security is enforced across three distinct layers:

  • Application framework level: TrueSource Spring Enterprise delivers continuous patch and dependency management, including commercial day-0 validated security-only patches from core Spring maintainers and clean-room builds of Java dependencies for Spring Boot. 
  • Platform level: Tanzu Platform enforces a deny-by-default runtime with an isolated credential store outside the execution sandbox, preventing prompt injection attacks, while an integrated AI gateway centralizes, audits, and rate-limits agent tool calling. 
  • Infrastructure level: VMware vDefend enforces zero-trust networking, micro-segmentation, and security policies at deployment time.

Together, these layers give engineering teams consistent, full-stack protection from underlying infrastructure up through the application and agent runtime. 

The Future State of Application Modernization

The path forward is a private cloud that adapts to how applications actually evolve. Broadcom continues to advance this platform with enhanced TCO optimization, efficient deployment and management of modern workloads, and stronger security for production AI workloads. Organizations gain a standardized, secure path to production that supports every workload, empowers developers, and boosts productivity. 

Ready to accelerate your app modernization journey? Dive into the resources below and discover how VCF can help your teams ship faster, simplify operations, and keep security built in: 

  • Product and Solution Pages: VMware Cloud Foundation, VCF Application Modernization, and VMware Tanzu Platform 
  • Read the latest App Modernization Solution Brief and Top 5 App Modernization Challenges ebook 
  • Blogs:
    • vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.8 Announcement 
    • Advancing Cloud-Native Ecosystems Through Open Collaboration
    • Broadcom at KubeCon North America 2026
    • Forrester TEI: See How Organizations Achieved 137% ROI with VMware Cloud Foundation 9
    • Introducing KubeVM Service: Why Declarative VM Management Matters Now
    • VCF 9.1: The Secure, Cost-Effective Private Cloud Platform for Production AI
  1. Broadcom Customer Survey, VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9 customers (n = 44), March 2026.

In this episode of VCF Breakroom Chats, Anika Suri (Product Marketing Engineer at Broadcom) and Harish Madhavan (Head of Global Partner Solutions at Kong) talk about the growing challenge of enterprise AI traffic governance, the security risks posed by autonomous agentic AI, and how combining Kong Gateway with VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) provides a unified traffic control plane to safely scale AI workloads.
Watch the full video below to catch the complete conversation!

Ready to take control of your enterprise AI traffic? Dive deeper into how Kong Gateway and VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) work together to secure and scale autonomous AI workloads. Explore the technical details and implementation strategies detailed in the Kong Konnect API and AI Gateway with VMware VKS blog, or get a comprehensive architectural overview by downloading the official technical white paper.

About the VCF Breakroom Chat Series

​In this series, we share vlogs with industry-recognized experts from Broadcom and Broadcom partners and customers. These vlogs are concise, like meeting in a breakroom and getting great information from a quick conversation. This series is for you if you are an IT practitioner: IT admin, cloud or platform architect, platform engineer, developer, DevOps, senior IT manager, IT executive, or AI/ML professional. 

If you are new to the series, please check out our previous episodes.
